h1: Can seam inspection for small canning lines
title: Can Seam Inspection on Small Lines | Craft Beer School
desc: How a double seam is formed, what to measure in a seam teardown, how often to check and the seam defects that leak or burst.
teaser: A can is only as good as a seam a few millimetres tall. Most small breweries check it far less often than they should.
standfirst: The double seam is what holds a can together under pressure. Small canning lines often run for hours without a proper check. Here is how the seam is formed, what to inspect and how often.
sections:
A can end is joined to the body by rolling the two metal edges together. The first operation roll curls the end's flange and the body's flange around each other. The second operation roll presses that curl flat and tight. The result is five layers of metal folded together with a sealing compound inside.

Get either roll wrong and the seam looks fine from a distance but leaks slowly, admits oxygen or fails under pressure. In a hot warehouse, a weak seam on a carbonated can is a real risk. So seam inspection is a safety check as much as a quality one.

A trained operator can catch many problems by eye and touch. Look at the seam all the way round for:

  • Droops, where part of the seam hangs lower than the rest.
  • Vees or lips, small points of metal sticking out below the seam.
  • Sharp edges or cut-overs at the top of the seam.
  • False seams, where the hooks have not engaged.
  • Spinners, where the end turns on the body.

A common pattern borrowed from food canning is a visual check on each seaming head roughly every 30 minutes while the line runs. On a small line with one or two heads, that takes a minute.

A teardown means cutting or stripping a seam to measure its inner structure. External measurements come first, then internal ones:

  • Seam thickness and seam length (also called height or width), with a seam micrometer.
  • Countersink depth, from the top of the seam to the end panel.
  • Body hook and cover hook lengths.
  • Overlap, how far the hooks overlap each other.
  • Tightness, judged from wrinkles on the cover hook.

Your can and end supplier provides target ranges for their products. Use those, not generic numbers. A seam saw and projection system makes internal measurements faster and more accurate, but careful manual teardown with a micrometer works for a small line.

Common practice is a full teardown on every seaming head at start-up, after any jam or adjustment, when changing end or can supplier and at fixed intervals during the run, often every few hours. A small brewery canning for one shift might tear down at start, mid-run and end.

Write each result on a record sheet against the targets. Trends matter. A body hook that shortens steadily over a month points to wearing rolls or chuck long before the seam fails.
Seaming and the rest of the line

Seam quality depends on more than the seamer. Fill level affects headspace and how the end sits. Undercover gassing affects oxygen. Our guide to fill level checks covers the first. Hygiene also matters: beer and sugar on the seaming chuck and rolls cause slipping and damage. Clean them on schedule, as in our guide to cleaning in place.

Mobile canning services are common in India. If you use one, ask for their seam records for your run and keep them. They are your evidence if a market complaint arrives.

A slow leak may not show for days. Hold a few cans from every run, upside down, at warm temperature and check for weeping, loss of pressure or stickiness. Oxygen can enter through a weak seam too, so poor seams can show up as stale beer. Plating samples from leaking cans, as in our guide to microbiology plating, tells you whether spoilage organisms got in as well.
Set up a seam log today

Get your can supplier's seam specification sheet if you do not have it. Create a record sheet with each measurement, its target range and space for each head and time. On your next run, do a visual check every 30 minutes and a teardown at start and end.

Train at least two people to do teardowns, so a holiday or a sick day does not mean a run without checks. Seam inspection is a skill that improves with practice. The first few teardowns are slow, then they become routine.

Keep the torn-down cans for a week with the record sheet. If a question comes up, you can measure them again.
faqs: How often should I check can seams?
A common pattern is a visual check every 30 minutes per seaming head and a full teardown at start-up, after any jam or adjustment and every few hours.
What is measured in a can seam teardown?
Seam thickness, seam length, countersink depth, body hook, cover hook, overlap and tightness, compared against the can supplier's specification.
What does a droop on a can seam mean?
Part of the seam hangs lower than the rest, often from a filling or seaming problem. It can mean poor overlap there, so investigate and tear down a sample.
